paras: The lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James was the shooting of two Black prisoners by a mob at the railroad depot in Madison, Florida, on the morning of August 25, 1882. The men, convicted of the 1881 killing of Frank Patterson but granted a new trial, were being taken under a sheriff's guard to Jasper for retrial when armed men stopped the train and shot them. Governor William D. Bloxham offered a $5,000 reward, but a coroner's jury found that they died at the hands of parties unknown, and no one was reported tried.

Savage and James were convicted of first-degree murder on June 26, 1881, for the killing of Frank Patterson, described as a Madison lawyer, on February 8, 1881, in a room where testimony was being taken in the Bisbee vs. Finley election contest. According to a Tallahassee correspondent, the Governor had then sent three companies of volunteers to guard the Madison jail until the legislature allowed the prisoners to be moved to Tallahassee for safekeeping. After the State Supreme Court granted a new trial in April 1882, a special term of the Hamilton County Circuit Court was set to try them at Jasper on August 29.

Sheriff Altman of Hamilton County came for them with a guard of four and moved them on Friday rather than Saturday or Monday as expected, having been told by Sheriff Hankins on Thursday that he need fear no trouble. The same Friday, William Bryan was to have been hanged at Madison, but his execution had been stayed by a writ of error.

Before the 9:05 passenger train arrived, depot agent W. S. Jordan tried to telegraph Greenville to have it stopped and found the wires cut both ways. He and the conductor signaled the engineer to go on, but someone had uncoupled the baggage car and passenger coach. Jordan saw about one hundred men, none disguised, rush toward the train, and the Jacksonville wire reported that twelve or fifteen of them went inside, while the Madison Recorder and the sheriff put the number at about twenty.

Altman said the armed men rushed over him and his guard and opened fire, and Savage fell dead at his feet. James, though shackled, ran out the back door toward town, pursued by men firing volley after volley, and fell dead at the southeast corner of Captain J. L. Inglis' pasture with shot through his face and head. Altman's brother, one of the guards, was wounded in the thigh, and the car was riddled with bullets, though no passenger was reported killed.

Judge R. R. Witherspoon empaneled a jury of inquest shortly after 11 o'clock, and the bodies were turned over to the men's families at 3 o'clock. At the same hour white and Black residents met at the courthouse under Judge E. J. Vann and adopted resolutions condemning a 'heinous crime' committed by persons unknown to them, while leading Black men gave assurances that their people would attempt no violence. On August 26 Bloxham proclaimed a reward of $5,000 for the arrest and conviction of the killers.

The inquest sat behind closed doors and subpoenaed witnesses as far away as Jacksonville, most of them Black, and on September 6 it returned a verdict of death at the hands of parties unknown. The Live Oak Bulletin reported that Sheriff Altman had been warned in Madison not to testify, or he would probably be killed. Black residents called an indignation meeting in Tallahassee, and another was held in Jacksonville to denounce the killing.

The matter was left to the Madison County grand jury at the October term under State Attorney Blackwell, after the Floridian rejected a Jacksonville Times call for the Governor to guarantee witnesses protection in advance. By September 30 the Volusia Enterprise Herald wrote that the affair 'seems to have reached a termination', and no indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Jacksonville dispatch ran the same day in papers from Dakota to Texas under headlines such as 'Riddled with Bullets', with the Waco Daily Examiner printing Savage's name as 'Lanage'. Summary columns reduced it to a line, the Richmond Dispatch heading it 'Two Convicted Murderers Riddled with Bullets by a Mob' and the Yorkville Enquirer saying the prisoners were 'assassinated'. A Kentucky weekly wrongly placed the killing near Jacksonville and said the men were taken out and hanged.

Florida papers condemned the killing, and the Tallahassee Floridian called it the murder 'in cold blood' of prisoners in the hands of the law, while faulting Dennis Eagan and attorney J. N. Stripling for not warning the Governor of a plot Eagan said he knew of two weeks earlier. The Savannah Morning News's Tallahassee correspondent deplored lynch law but blamed outsiders in town for Bryan's hanging and worried that the 'partisan press of the North' would use the case to discourage immigration. A Jacksonville letter in the same paper noted that some parties were trying to make political capital of the killing.

The case also became a quarrel between regions of the state, as the Jacksonville Times warned strangers away from Madison while the crime went 'unwhipt of justice'. The Floridian answered that the animosity had 'exhausted itself' with the killing and pointed to unpunished crimes in East and South Florida, and the Volusia Enterprise Herald replied that Madison was a disgrace to the state.

The Tallahassee correspondent held that the people of Madison were blameless and that the crowd gathered for Bryan's execution did the work, a view the depot clerk P. S. Coggins echoed only as a supposition about who the crowd were. A Savannah report of September 5 that two men had been arrested as participants was followed two days later by an account placing the same arrests in the Neff murder case in Volusia County.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James
bases: A crowd stopped a train at Madison and a party of armed men shot dead two Black prisoners in a sheriff's custody on their way to a retrial (A5, A16, A17, A18).

Twelve to twenty armed men, out of a crowd of about one hundred, took two prisoners from a sheriff's guard and shot them to death with no lawful authority (A5, A17, A18); a Tallahassee letter said the crowd acted because the men 'had been condemned to die' for the killing of Frank Patterson (A24).

The Jacksonville wire, the local Madison Recorder account with the sheriff's and depot agent's statements, the Governor's proclamation and the coroner's verdict all agree on the core event (A5, A16, A17, A18, A31).

accounts.gist: About one hundred people met the train at Madison and twelve or fifteen rushed in and riddled the prisoners with bullets after the wires were cut and the rear cars uncoupled.

accounts.label: Madison Recorder and local witnesses
accounts.gist: About twenty armed men rushed past the sheriff's guard, killed Savage in the car and chased the shackled James up toward town, firing volleys until he fell; none of the crowd was disguised.

accounts.label: Tallahassee correspondent
accounts.gist: Madison residents were blameless; outsiders who had gathered for Bryan's hanging, learning it was stayed, decided Savage and James should die as sentenced.

accounts.label: Kentucky brief
accounts.gist: A train near Jacksonville was stopped by a mob and two prisoners were taken out and hanged.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Jacksonville dispatch under heads like 'Riddled with Bullets' and 'Two Men Riddled With Bullets by An Avenging Mob'.
The Tallahassee Floridian called it a murder 'in cold blood' of prisoners in custody and demanded that Madison find the killers.
The Savannah paper's Tallahassee correspondent deplored lynch law but called the victims 'poor wretches', blamed outsiders and worried about Northern 'partisan press' and immigration.
The Jacksonville Times, quoted in the Floridian, warned strangers away from Madison while the crime went unpunished; the Floridian called this an attack on Middle Florida.
